{"synthesis": "# Library-first vs. moon-first: resolving §0.1

**Summary of the recommendation.** Take **Option C**, but with a much narrower definition of "library-first" than §0.1 currently implies. The evidence from release-please, Nx Release, semantic-release, and knope does *not* support Option B's premise — that callisto has three equally-weighted consumers — because callisto's own design has already decided the GitHub Action is a bash-composite that shells out to the CLI binary (§12.1), not an independent API consumer. That leaves exactly two real consumers: `callisto-cli` and `callisto-moon`, and the second is better understood as a *second compilation target* (`wasm32-wasip1`, no `tokio`/`reqwest`, no `sh -c`) than a second API surface. What the prior art actually validates is not consumer symmetry but **seam placement**: Nx's v21 rewrite was caused by ecosystem I/O logic being smeared into coordination logic, and knope's cascade is permanently trapped inside its binary crate. So: keep the coordination core moon-free and binary-free as a hard, CI-enforced rule; ship moon as the one blessed integration; and do *not* pay for a stable public Rust API, a C ABI, or dyn-compatible traits before v1.0. One concrete correction falls out of this: `MoonProjectGraphResolver` as specced in §15 is the wrong shape and should be deleted — moon's project graph structurally cannot supply the data §7.4's cascade rules need.

---

## Recommendation: Option C — library-first internals, moon as the single reference integration

### Option B's premise is already false in callisto's own design

§0.1 frames Option B as "moon integration, the GitHub Action, and the standalone CLI are three independent, equally thin consumers." §12.1 of the same document already decided the Action is "composite (bash-in-YAML), not TypeScript," whose logic is "`gh` CLI calls, `callisto` CLI calls, and branching on JSON." That is not a library consumer. It is a *CLI* consumer, and it consumes the `--format json` contract, not a Rust API.

This distinction is exactly what the release-please analogy hides. release-please's Action genuinely is a second library consumer — `release-please-action/src/index.ts:16` does `import {GitHub, Manifest, CreatedRelease, PullRequest, VERSION} from 'release-please'` and calls the same `Manifest.fromConfig`/`fromManifest` the CLI does. But that is nearly free for release-please, because the Action and the library are both Node in the same runtime: importing the library costs one line. For callisto, the equivalent would be a Rust or napi-bound Action binary, and §12.1 explicitly rejected that on supply-chain and auditability grounds. So release-please's proof of "N equally-weighted consumers" does not transfer; it is an artifact of a single-runtime ecosystem.

There is a second reason the release-please analogy transfers less than it looks. `Manifest.fromManifest` does not read a working tree — `parseConfig`/`parseReleasedVersions` (`src/manifest.ts:444-449`) fetch config and manifest JSON through `github.getFileContentsOnBranch(...)`. release-please's world model is a remote-addressable SCM. Its library-first shape bought portability across *hosting* consumers, all of which talk to the same GitHub API. Callisto's consumers all operate on a local checkout with a local project graph. The axis release-please's abstraction was built to span is not an axis callisto has.

Finally, §16 licenses the coordination core AGPL-3.0 with CLA. `callisto-graph` — the crate whose reusability Option B is meant to protect — is a crate almost nobody will build a third-party integration against, by deliberate design. Option B's ecosystem-of-consumers value proposition is licensed out of existence by callisto's own license posture. Only `callisto-format` and `callisto-model` are MIT/Apache, and those are the two crates whose reusability nobody is arguing about.

### But Option A is genuinely dangerous, and knope shows exactly how

knope is the closest structural analogue to callisto that exists (Rust, Cargo + npm dual-published packages, changeset files, `versioned_files` as the base abstraction), and it is a clean cautionary tale. `crates/knope-versioning/src/lib.rs` declares six modules — `action`, `changes`, `package`, `release_notes`, `semver`, `versioned_file` — and there is no `workspace`, `graph`, or `cascade` module anywhere in the library. The entire multi-package cascade mechanism lives in `crates/knope/src/config/package.rs` as two functions, `cargo_workspace()` (lines ~150-184) and `npm_workspaces()` (lines ~186-260), which scan every workspace member's manifest for sibling references and append them to that package's `versioned_files` list so they get rewritten in lockstep. There is no `pub` graph type, no `DependencyGraph`, no reusable API. A second consumer — an editor plugin, a CI action, a moon extension — cannot reach any of it without vendoring that file.

Nx's evidence points the same direction from a different angle. The v21 rewrite (`nrwl/nx#30418`) replaced `ReleaseVersionGenerator` with `VersionActions` (`packages/nx/src/command-line/release/version/version-actions.ts`) precisely because generic logic — git-tag resolution, bump application, cross-group dependent traversal, version-data bookkeeping — had been duplicated per ecosystem plugin and diverged. The bug list Nx attributes to that architecture is a list of exactly callisto's problem domain: cross-release-group dependents not bumped (#21466), duplicate version-data keys when two groups touch one project (#26444, #30363), independent versioning over-incrementing a dependent once per changed dependency instead of once total (#27823), workspace/file-protocol specs not rewritten before publish (#28049). Note that all of these are *coordination* bugs caused by *ecosystem* code owning coordination decisions. Nx's own PR states the fix as a rule: "No core business logic about releases is handled within a `VersionActions` implementation."

That rule is the transferable lesson, and it is a statement about seams, not about consumers. Nx also validated the new abstraction end-to-end against exactly one blessed integration (JS, dogfooded on angular-eslint) before flipping the default in v21 — and even so, early `VersionActions` adopters in 20.8 ate a breaking interface change (`manifestRootsToUpdate: string[]` → `manifestsToUpdate: {manifestPath, preserveLocalDependencyProtocols}[]`) before v21 stabilized. Nx's own team needed two iterations to place the seam correctly *with* a real consumer to test against. Designing three equally-weighted consumer surfaces up front, against two hypothetical consumers, would be strictly worse odds.

semantic-release closes the argument from the other side: a clean library API is necessary but not sufficient. `index.js` exports a callable async function and `cli.js` is a thin yargs wrapper — textbook library-first — and monorepo support *still* had to be built externally (`@qiwi/multi-semantic-release` does `import semanticRelease from "semantic-release"` and wraps the whole thing), because the nine-hook lifecycle in `lib/definitions/plugins.js` extends *what each step does* and cannot change *which packages are processed or when*. The orchestration loop must live in the core. For callisto that means: aggregation (§7.1), graph construction (§7.2), cascade-to-fixpoint (§7.4), group alignment (§7.5), and mutation ordering (§7.6) all belong in library crates, and no integration — moon included — may own any part of that loop. This is P6 restated, and it is the one thing that is non-negotiable under any option.

### The minimal version of library-first, and why it captures ~all the benefit

Yes, there is a minimal version, and it is the right one. It is four CI-enforceable rules, not an API design project:

1. **Zero moon in the dependency tree of the core.** `callisto-format`, `callisto-model`, `callisto-graph`, `callisto-manifests`, `callisto-conventional`, `callisto-changelog` must not depend on `callisto-moon` or on any moon crate, transitively. Enforce with a CI step, not a convention.
2. **The core must build for `wasm32-wasip1`.** This is the real forcing function, and it is better than a hypothetical second consumer because it fails loudly at compile time. A core crate that reaches for `tokio`, `reqwest`, `std::process::Command`, or filesystem walks that assume a real OS breaks the moon build immediately. §11 and §9.5 already made this achievable by removing the publish executor; make it a job in CI from v0.1, before `callisto-moon` exists.
3. **Compute/apply split, borrowed verbatim from release-please.** `Manifest.buildPullRequests()` / `createPullRequests()` and `buildReleases()` / `createReleases()` (`src/manifest.ts`) is the single most transferable idea in the prior art: every command is a pure function returning a plan value, plus a separate applier that touches disk. Every CLI handler in `src/bin/release-please.ts:483-566` is literally construct-manifest → call one `build*`/`create*` → print. If callisto adopts that split, consumer equivalence is a *consequence* rather than something you design for.
4. **The stable public contract is the JSON plan, not the Rust API.** §9.2 already has `schemaVersion`; §P7 already demands "a versioned, fixtured JSON/API contract" at every boundary. Commit to the JSON as the supported surface, fixture it, and explicitly document the Rust API of AGPL crates as unstable pre-1.0. This is what lets you take an Nx-style breaking interface change in `DependencyResolver` at v0.3 without it being an ecosystem event.

Everything Option B would add beyond this — a C ABI, semver-stabilized Rust APIs, dyn-compatible traits, a plugin registration surface analogous to release-please's `factories/plugin-factory.ts` — is cost with no identified beneficiary. And release-please shows the symmetry doesn't hold anyway even when you try: `Bootstrapper` (`src/bootstrapper.ts`), which implements the `bootstrap` command, is imported directly by the CLI (`src/bin/release-please.ts:32`) and is **not** re-exported from `src/index.ts`. A capability that matters — first-run config generation — never made it to the public API in a codebase that is otherwise a model of library-first discipline. Assume the same will happen to callisto and decide up front what is *allowed* to be CLI-only glue (`completions`, `tag` per §11's table, interactive `init` prompts) rather than discovering it as a violated principle.

---

## Crate-boundary implications

**Before (§15, provisional):** eight crates — `callisto-format`, `callisto-model`, `callisto-graph`, `callisto-manifests`, `callisto-conventional`, `callisto-changelog`, `callisto-cli`, `callisto-moon` — with `callisto-graph` exposing a `DependencyResolver` trait with two impls, `ManifestWalkResolver` and `MoonProjectGraphResolver`.

**Under "moon-first, don't overthink it" (Option A).** `callisto-model`, `callisto-graph`, `callisto-manifests`, `callisto-conventional`, and `callisto-changelog` collapse into one `callisto-core`, because with no consumer boundary to defend there is no reason to pay for five crate boundaries; only `callisto-format` survives separately as the MIT primitive. `DependencyResolver` disappears — you call `moon project-graph --json` directly and Q1 resolves to "moon is authoritative." `callisto-cli` grows a second, degraded discovery path (an `ignore`-crate walk) that is separately maintained and separately buggy. That is precisely knope's shape, and it is where knope's `cargo_workspace()`/`npm_workspaces()` ended up. The failure mode is not that you can't ship — knope shipped — it is that the moment you want a second surface you vendor or rewrite, and the two discovery paths drift, which is Nx's #21466/#28695 class of bug.

**Under "fully library-first" (Option B).** You add at least two crates and change trait shapes materially. A `callisto-plan` crate holding the plan/report value types and the JSON schema, licensed MIT/Apache since it is the public contract. A `callisto-ffi` (C ABI) or a stable WASM ABI crate for non-Rust consumers, plus the versioning policy and soundness testing that implies. `callisto-graph` plausibly splits into a pure-graph crate and a `callisto-cascade` policy crate so third parties can reuse the graph without inheriting callisto's cascade opinions. Most concretely: **`DependencyResolver` as written in §15 cannot survive.** Its methods return `impl Iterator<Item = &Package>` / `impl Iterator<Item = &DepEdge>`, which is RPITIT and therefore not dyn-compatible. A genuinely open plugin boundary requires `Box<dyn DependencyResolver>`, which forces every method to `Box<dyn Iterator<Item = …> + '_>` — the same shape `Manifest::iter_dependencies` already has. That is a real runtime and ergonomics cost paid to serve consumers who, under §16's AGPL, cannot legally exist in the commercial case anyway. `callisto-manifests`'s `Manifest` trait would likewise need to be publicly implementable and therefore frozen early.

**Under the recommendation (Option C).** The eight crates stay as-is. Four specific changes:

1. **Delete `MoonProjectGraphResolver`.** This is a correctness change, not a stylistic one. moon's project graph does not carry version requirements. In `moonrepo/moon@50d91a0`, `crates/config/src/project/dep_config.rs` defines `ProjectDependencyConfig { id: Id, scope: DependencyScope, source: DependencySource, via: Option<String> }` — `scope` is `Build | Development | Peer | Production | Root`, `source` is `Explicit | Implicit`, and `via` is provenance metadata. There is no version-requirement string anywhere on the edge, including for implicit edges injected by toolchain plugins through `ProjectGraphBuilder::extend_with_dependency` (`crates/project-builder/src/project_builder.rs:211-224`), which merely stamps `source = Implicit` on the same struct. §7.4's entire cascade table pivots on "spec covers new version," and §7.3's `DepSpec` requires the original spec string for lossless round-trip. moon cannot supply either. A `MoonProjectGraphResolver` would have to re-read the manifests to fill in what it's missing, at which point it *is* `ManifestWalkResolver`.

2. **Introduce a narrower trait — `ProjectLocator` — and make `ManifestWalkResolver` the only `DependencyResolver`.** What moon *does* provide, and provides better than an `ignore` walk, is authoritative project discovery: roots, ids, language/toolchain, and the explicit/implicit edge set as a cross-check. So the moon-shaped seam is `fn projects(&self) -> Result<Vec<ProjectRoot>, LocateError>` with two impls (`IgnoreWalkLocator` in `callisto-graph`, `MoonProjectLocator` in `callisto-moon`), plus an optional `fn declared_edges(&self) -> Option<Vec<(ProjectId, ProjectId, DependencyScope)>>` used purely for the §7.2 cross-check. This resolves **Q1** as *cross-check, definitively* — not as a preference but because moon's edge type lacks the field the cascade needs. It also shrinks the moon integration to something a WASM extension can actually do well, and it maps cleanly onto Nx's `VersionActions` rule: moon supplies discovery I/O, the core owns all coordination.

3. **`DependencyResolver` keeps `-> impl Iterator` and static dispatch.** No boxing, no dyn-compatibility, no pre-1.0 stability promise. Document `callisto-graph`'s Rust API as unstable in its README; the supported contract is `--format json` + `schemaVersion`.

4. **Plan/report types live in `callisto-model`, licensed MIT/Apache with `callisto-format`.** The §9.2 plan is the public contract per P7; putting it in the permissive tier means the Action, a future Nx plugin, and anyone writing a consumer can depend on the schema types without touching AGPL code. `callisto-cli` then contains only argv parsing, rendering, and process-level I/O — the release-please `bin/release-please.ts` shape — and mutation (§7.6 steps 3-8) lives in `callisto-manifests`/`callisto-changelog`, not in the binary crate.

Two optional, cheap additions: a `callisto-fixtures` dev-only crate holding the byte-compat corpus and plan-schema golden files shared by `callisto-cli` and `callisto-moon` tests (P7's "fixtured contract" made literal), and a CI rule that `callisto-cli/src` contains no graph construction or cascade code — the automated version of "don't become knope."

---

## Secondary question: group-priority / simultaneous release groups

**Confirmed: callisto does not need a group-priority mechanism, and pre-release mode is not why.**

release-please's `GroupPriority` plugin (`src/plugins/group-priority.ts:53-74`) is a post-processing filter over already-computed `CandidateReleasePullRequest[]`: it buckets candidates by `pullRequest.group`, walks a maintainer-ordered `groups: string[]`, and returns only the highest-priority non-empty bucket, discarding every lower-priority candidate for that run. It exists because release-please's `Manifest.buildPullRequests()` runs independent per-path strategies that can each independently decide "I want to release now," and `group` is a *label on candidates*, not a versioning constraint. Two labelled candidate sets can therefore collide and need arbitration — the canonical case being Java snapshot PRs vs. stable-release PRs.

Callisto's model forecloses this by construction, for three independent reasons. Fixed and linked groups (§7.5) are inputs to version *computation*, not labels on emitted candidates — members are forced to a shared version before any plan exists. Callisto emits exactly one plan per invocation; there is no multi-strategy pass that can produce competing candidate sets. And §8 makes `--snapshot` and pre-mode mutually exclusive, which is precisely the dual-track scenario `GroupPriority` arbitrates.

So the answer is not "pre-release mode covers it" — pre-mode is single-track and is itself one of the reasons the collision can't arise. The correct framing is that callisto has no dual-channel concept at all. Two follow-ons:

- **Add config-parse-time validation instead of runtime arbitration** (P5): a package must belong to at most one fixed group and at most one linked group, and fixed ∩ linked must be empty. Reject at parse time with a clear error. Multi-group membership is the closest analogue to release-please's colliding-labels problem, and rejecting it is strictly better than arbitrating it.
- **Heed the `#2207` lesson about identity resolution.** `googleapis/release-please#2207` (Node project wrapping a Rust workspace — structurally callisto's case F) has sat open since Jan 2024 with no maintainer comment; `linked-versions` silently no-ops under `include-component-in-tag: false`, and the two candidate fixes (`#1749` open since March 2023, `#2211` closed unmerged) were never reviewed. `LinkedVersions.preconfigure()` keys off `strategiesByPath` while component identity is derived through tag-parsing logic that the tag-inclusion flag perturbs — two code paths for one concept. For callisto: `PackageId` → tag name resolution must be **one function** in `callisto-model`, used identically by §7.5 group forcing, `plan-publish`'s `releases[].tagName`, and the §P2 stateless `last_tag_for` primitive. If `tag_template` (§5.1) can change a package's identity for one of those three and not the others, you have rebuilt #2207.
- **Revisit only if** callisto ever adds a genuine dual-channel feature (same package, two cadenced release lines from the same commits) or relaxes the pre/snapshot mutual exclusion. Note the trigger in the design doc so the decision is revisitable rather than forgotten.

---

## Secondary question: 0.x remap rigidity (§6.2)

**Revised — but not in the direction the research implied.** Keep §6.2 rigid and unconditional. Add the opt-in one layer up, in §7.1's inference, never in `bump_version`.

The case for adding a `bumpMinorPreMajor` equivalent is real: it originates in `googleapis/release-please#558`, opened by a user citing SemVer's clause-4 carve-out and the Rust API guidelines' `C-STABLE` as the reason libraries are deliberately held at 0.x — verbatim callisto's audience. `DefaultVersioningStrategy` (`src/versioning-strategies/default.ts:27-105`) implements both `bumpMinorPreMajor` and `bumpPatchForMinorPreMajor`, defaulting to `false`, rerouting breaking → `MinorVersionUpdate` and `feat` → `PatchVersionUpdate` when `version.isPreMajor`. And the demand has been sustained: #2087 ("initial version 0.0.0 means pre-major options are not respected," still open, `help wanted`) and #2635 ("pre-major settings being ignored," Dec 2025) show the feature is load-bearing enough that people file bugs about it years later.

But applying that directly to §6.2 would be a mistake, for two reasons.

**First, P1 forbids it.** §6.2 is not merely "our bump function" — it is the byte-compat semantic contract with `@changesets/cli`, and P1 says the adoption gate overrides everything. A remap flag means callisto computes a *different version* than `@changesets/cli` from the *identical* changeset files. That destroys one-commit rollback, which is the whole adoption story. Byte-compatibility of files without semantic equivalence of computation is a trap: the files round-trip, the versions don't.

**Second, and more interesting: release-please's flag corrects an *inference*, not an explicit human decision.** In release-please, "major" arrives because a commit said `feat!:` — the human never chose a bump level, so remapping is a reasonable correction of a heuristic. In callisto, `major` in a changeset frontmatter is a human typing `major` next to a package name. Silently turning that into `0.6.0` overrides stated intent, and it is exactly the "why did my patch bump become a minor" surprise that generated #2635.

Callisto does, however, have release-please's actual situation: `ReleaseTrigger::Auto` (§5.1, §7.1) infers severity from conventional commits when no changeset names the package. **That** is where the flag belongs. Concretely:

- `callisto-format`'s `bump_version` stays exactly as §6.2 specifies — `0.5.2 + major → 1.0.0`, no exceptions, no flag, no config reaching it. It stays in the MIT crate as the canonical Rust implementation of changesets semantics, and its fixtures stay a pure byte/behavior-compat suite.
- Add an opt-in inference policy in `callisto-conventional`, per-package or per-group, e.g. `pre-major-inference = "conservative"`, that maps `breaking → Severity::Minor` and (separately gated) `feat → Severity::Patch` **when producing a severity for an `Auto`-trigger package whose current version is `0.y.z` with `y > 0`**. Default off.
- §7.1's existing rule — "a changeset always wins over inference" — means an explicit `major` still produces `1.0.0` under any setting. That is the right semantics and it falls out for free.
- **Specify the bootstrap interaction explicitly**, because that is where release-please is still leaking bugs three years on. If the current version is `0.0.z`, or there is no prior tag, the policy is inert: no remap, and the tool says so. #558's original thread traced failures to `defaultInitialVersion` defaulting to `v1.0.0` regardless of the flag; #2087 is the same disagreement at `0.0.0`. Callisto's §P2 stateless detection makes "no tag yet" a routine state, so this must be a tested case from day one, not an emergent one.
- **Document the divergence loudly.** `@changesets/cli` has no remap concept. Anything callisto infers that changesets couldn't have inferred is a divergence, and the migration guide (v0.4) should say so in the same breath as the one-commit-rollback promise — rollback is only lossless for `Changeset`-trigger packages.

Net effect: callisto gets the feature its Rust audience asks for, structurally cannot reproduce release-please's #558/#2087/#2635 bug class (because the remap never touches the bump primitive and never overrides explicit intent), and P1 stays intact.

---

Moon does provide dependency info — just not the specific slice callisto's cascade logic needs.

What moon's project graph gives you: **which projects depend on which**, with a `scope` (build/development/peer/production/root) and whether the edge is `explicit` (declared) or `implicit` (inferred by a toolchain plugin, e.g. from parsing `Cargo.toml`/`package.json` itself). If moon's edge type is just `{id, scope, source, via}` with no spec field, moon can tell you *that* A depends on B, but not *what range* A declared — so callisto still has to read the manifest itself to get the one piece of data the cascade actually computes against. At that point, using moon's graph as the resolver doesn't save the manifest read; it just adds a cross-check on top of it.

Still running in the background — I'll answer from the design as it already stands, which is exactly the fallback path for "no moon available."

This is what `ManifestWalkResolver` is for (§7.2/§15). Callisto builds its dependency graph **entirely from reading manifests directly** — it never actually needs moon to construct the graph; moon (if present) was only ever proposed as a second opinion.

Concretely, for each `Canonical` manifest callisto discovers (via `callisto.toml`'s `[[package-set]]` globs, or an `ignore`-crate walk of the workspace if no config exists yet), it:

1. **Parses the manifest itself** — `Cargo.toml`'s `[dependencies]`/`[dev-dependencies]`/`[build-dependencies]`, `package.json`'s `dependencies`/`devDependencies`/`peerDependencies`/`optionalDependencies`.
2. **Extracts a `DepSpec` per edge** (§7.3) — parsing each range string into `Exact`, `Range(VersionReq, original_string)`, `Workspace(WorkspaceKind)` (pnpm `workspace:*`), `Catalog`, `CargoBare`, or falling back to `Opaque` if it can't confidently round-trip. The original string is always kept alongside the parsed form specifically so a later rewrite doesn't corrupt anything it doesn't fully understand.
3. **Resolves package identity** across the two ecosystems (§5.4 — bare name if unambiguous, `cargo/foo`/`npm/foo` if the same name appears in both) to match edges to nodes.
4. **Assembles the graph** — nodes are packages, edges carry `DepKind` (Runtime/Dev/Peer/Optional/Build) + the `DepSpec` — with no external process invoked at all. Pure file I/O plus parsing.

This is also *why* the whole thing works in WASM/WASI (§11) — no `moon project-graph --json` shell-out, no `git`, nothing beyond reading files that are already in the workspace checkout. `ManifestWalkResolver` is the one and only resolver in the "under the recommendation (Option C)" plan from the decision doc — moon's role shrinks to an optional `ProjectLocator` used purely to cross-check that the manifest walk didn't miss a project, not to supply graph data itself.

So a non-moon system loses nothing functionally: it's the same code path moon-based usage runs, just without the extra cross-check step. That symmetry is precisely the point of keeping `callisto-graph` moon-agnostic.

input.new_string:
1. **Delete `MoonProjectGraphResolver`.** This is a correctness change, not a stylistic one. moon's project graph does not carry version requirements. `crates/config/src/project/dep_config.rs` defines `ProjectDependencyConfig { id: Id, scope: DependencyScope, source: DependencySource, via: Option<String> }` — `scope` is `Build | Development | Peer | Production | Root`, `source` is `Explicit | Implicit`, and `via` is provenance metadata. There is no version-requirement string anywhere on the edge or its `ProjectDependsOn` wrapper, including for implicit edges injected by toolchain plugins through `ProjectGraphBuilder::extend_with_dependency` (`crates/project-builder/src/project_builder.rs:211-224`), which merely stamps `source = Implicit` on the same struct — verified independently against both current `main` and the tree at commit `50d91a0` (a docs-only commit that happens to be current tip-of-main at time of writing, not one that touched this file; cite it only as "state of main as of writing," not as the commit that introduced the struct). §7.4's entire cascade table pivots on "spec covers new version," and §7.3's `DepSpec` requires the original spec string for lossless round-trip. moon cannot supply either. A `MoonProjectGraphResolver` would have to re-read the manifests to fill in what it's missing, at which point it *is* `ManifestWalkResolver`.

2. **Introduce a narrower trait — `ProjectLocator` — for discovery, and treat edge cross-checking as a separate, lossy-mapped concern.** This actually resolves two different sub-questions from §18 Q1, not one:
   - **Q1a (discovery — moon is authoritative when present).** `fn projects(&self) -> Result<Vec<ProjectRoot>, LocateError>`, with `IgnoreWalkLocator` in `callisto-graph` and `MoonProjectLocator` in `callisto-moon`. When moon is available its project roots supersede the `ignore` walk outright — this is where moon adds real, unambiguous value (catching an implicit edge or a `moon.yml`-declared project the manifest walk has no way to see at all).
   - **Q1b (edges — cross-check only, explicitly lossy).** An optional `fn declared_edges(&self) -> Option<Vec<DeclaredEdge>>` where `DeclaredEdge` is a **callisto-owned** type in `callisto-model` (`{from: ProjectId, to: ProjectId, kind: DeclaredEdgeKind, via: Option<String>}`) — not moon's `DependencyScope` reused under a colliding name, which would either violate rule 1 (moon type leaking into the core's dependency tree) or silently drop the fact that the mapping is lossy: moon has `Root` and no `Optional`; moon's `Production` doesn't cleanly separate from callisto's `Runtime`+`Optional` split, which matters specifically for the napi `optionalDependencies` pattern §7.5 exists to serve. `MoonProjectLocator` owns an explicit, documented `DependencyScope → DeclaredEdgeKind` mapping; the cross-check compares edge *presence* (plus `via` for a human-readable diagnostic), never kind equality. Disagreement policy: warn by default, `--strict-graph` hard-fails, and surface it as a field in `--format json` output so the Action/moon workflow can gate on it — this is what makes §18 Q1's "disagreement is itself a useful diagnostic" promise real instead of silently dropped.

   This also shrinks the moon integration to something a WASM extension can actually do well, and maps cleanly onto Nx's `VersionActions` rule: moon supplies discovery I/O, the core owns all coordination. One risk to name rather than discover later: `ProjectLocator`'s shape is exactly the kind of trait Nx's own `VersionActions` rewrite shows breaking under a real second consumer (`manifestRootsToUpdate: string[]` → `manifestsToUpdate: {...}` inside one Nx minor). Treat `ProjectLocator`/`declared_edges` as expected to break pre-1.0, and prefer a versioned DTO (`callisto-moon` producing a `ProjectSet` value type owned by `callisto-model`) over a long-lived trait contract where practical — data contracts version more gracefully than trait signatures. `callisto-moon` should pin a specific moon compatibility range accordingly.

3. **`DependencyResolver` keeps `-> impl Iterator` and static dispatch, and needs a named second implementor to justify keeping the trait at all.** No boxing, no dyn-compatibility, no pre-1.0 stability promise — but after change 1 deletes `MoonProjectGraphResolver`, `ManifestWalkResolver` is the *only* implementor, and a one-implementor trait is exactly the "cost with no identified beneficiary" this doc argues against for Option B elsewhere. The legitimate second implementor is a fixture/in-memory resolver for the `callisto-fixtures` golden-test suite (construct a graph from literal `Package`/`DepEdge` values, no filesystem, for cascade unit tests) — keep the trait and name that as the reason. If that suite ends up not needing one, demote `DependencyResolver` to a concrete `ManifestWalkResolver` struct and let §15's "moon-agnostic core" commitment be carried by the CI rule in rule 1 instead of by trait shape. Document `callisto-graph`'s Rust API as unstable in its README either way; the supported contract is `--format json` + `schemaVersion` on stdout.

All stale phrasing is gone (grep found nothing, confirming the fixes took). The doc now incorporates the red-team findings:

**Verification: all 3 fact-checks CONFIRMED** — moon's `ProjectDependencyConfig` genuinely has no version field, release-please's `Bootstrapper` genuinely never made it to the public API, RPITIT is genuinely non-dyn-compatible with no escape hatch. The recommendation itself survives.

**8 issues fixed in the doc:**
1. Rule 2's "forcing function" was overstated (WASI compiles `std::fs`/`Command` fine, only fails at runtime) — now specifies wasmtime fixture runs, not just `cargo build`, and names the exec/path seams the core actually needs.
2. `declared_edges()` was leaking moon's own `DependencyScope` type into the "moon-free" core — now a callisto-owned `DeclaredEdgeKind` with an explicit, lossy-aware mapping.
3. The AGPL/licensing argument was decorative and overclaimed ("cannot legally exist") — cut to one accurate sentence; the real argument is the Nx/knope/semantic-release evidence, not licensing.
4. After deleting `MoonProjectGraphResolver`, `DependencyResolver` had exactly one implementor left — the doc's own "no beneficiary" test applied to itself. Now names the fixture-resolver as the second implementor, or says to demote to a concrete struct.
5. "Second compilation target, not API surface" was contradicted by the doc's own new `ProjectLocator` trait — reframed honestly as two consumers with an asymmetric seam.
6. §18 Q1 got mislabeled as one answer when it's really two (discovery: moon authoritative; edges: cross-check) — split, with an explicit disagreement policy (warn/`--strict-graph`/exposed in JSON).
7. Rule 4 pointed at `.callisto/plan.json`, which §7.6/§13 explicitly say is non-load-bearing — corrected to stdout `--format json`.
8. "P1 forbids it" overclaimed a citation for what's actually a reasonable *extension* of P1 — restated as applying only to `Changeset`-trigger packages, reconciling it with the doc's own later concession about `Auto`-trigger packages.

Plus a citation-hygiene pass (moon commit SHA, release-please line numbers, knope's actual private function names) and one flagged-but-not-yet-fixed structural risk worth your attention: the doc now explicitly says `ProjectLocator` should be expected to break pre-1.0 (same failure class as Nx's `VersionActions` interface break) and recommends a versioned DTO over a long-lived trait where practical.
Did we learn anything from release-please or other alternatives?

Yes — beyond just resolving §0.1, the research produced several concrete, reusable lessons that changed specific parts of callisto's design, not just the top-level architecture call:

**From release-please:**
- **The compute/apply split is worth stealing outright.** `Manifest.buildPullRequests()`/`createPullRequests()` and `buildReleases()`/`createReleases()` — every command is a pure function returning a plan value, then a separate step that touches disk. This is now baked into the decision doc's rule 3 and is arguably the single most actionable idea from all four tools.
- **Generic cascade logic factored out of ecosystem plugins works.** `WorkspacePlugin`'s shared base class does ~85% of the graph/topo-sort/merge work; `CargoWorkspace`/`NodeWorkspace` are thin format adapters. Directly validates callisto's format/model/graph crate split.
- **Even disciplined library-first code accumulates CLI-only glue.** `Bootstrapper` never made it into the public API despite everything else being clean. Lesson applied: decide *up front* what's allowed to be CLI-only (callisto's `completions`, `tag`, interactive `init`) instead of discovering the violation later.
- **The `#2207` bug (unfixed 2 years)** taught a specific, non-obvious lesson: it's not that cross-ecosystem "bump everything together" is architecturally hard — it's that release-please has *two independent code paths* computing "package identity" (grouping logic vs. tag-inclusion resolution) that silently disagree. Directly produced the rule that `PackageId → tag name` must be one function in `callisto-model`, used identically everywhere.
- **`bumpMinorPreMajor` has real, sustained demand** from exactly callisto's audience (Rust `C-STABLE` 0.x discipline) but has been buggy for years specifically at the "no tag yet" bootstrap boundary. Callisto's answer — add it only to conventional-commit *inference*, never to `bump_version` itself, and test the no-tag case from day one — sidesteps that whole bug class rather than importing it.
- **Release-please's world model is remote-SCM (fetches config over the GitHub API), not local-checkout.** This is a "so what" that limits the whole analogy: its library-first payoff is portability across *hosting* consumers, an axis callisto doesn't have.

**From Nx Release's v21 rewrite** — the single most valuable data point, because it's a well-resourced team's real "we got the seam wrong the first time": duplicating coordination logic per-ecosystem-plugin (instead of one shared core) produced a specific, recognizable bug class — cross-group dependents not bumped, duplicate version-data keys, over-incrementing dependents, stale workspace-protocol specs. That's almost a checklist of failure modes callisto's cascade logic (§7.4) needs to guard against structurally. Also: even Nx needed two iterations to get the abstraction boundary right, *with* a real consumer to test against — which is direct evidence against callisto trying to design three symmetric consumer surfaces up front with only hypothetical ones.

**From semantic-release:** a clean library API is necessary but *not sufficient* — monorepo support still had to live outside the library entirely (`multi-semantic-release` wraps the whole thing) because its 9-hook plugin lifecycle can only change *what each step does*, not *which packages get processed or in what order*. That's the concrete argument for P6 (release semantics live in the core, never in a wrapper): if the orchestration loop itself became a plugin concern, callisto would hit the same wall.

**From knope** — the cautionary tale for Option A: it's the closest Rust structural analogue, and its entire multi-package cascade lives as two *private* functions inside the CLI binary crate, with no reusable graph type at all. That's not a hypothetical risk — it's what happens by default if you don't deliberately pull cascade logic into a library crate.

**One meta-lesson**, arguably the most useful outcome of the whole exercise: comparing callisto's own design against these tools surfaced an internal inconsistency callisto's authors hadn't noticed — §0.1 argued Option B on the premise of "three equally-weighted consumers," but §12.1 (written earlier in the same doc) had already decided the GitHub Action is a bash CLI-wrapper, not a library consumer. The research didn't just answer the question posed; it caught the doc contradicting itself.

content.text:
**The mechanism already in the design (§5.1, §7.1, §14):**

```rust
enum ReleaseTrigger {
    Changeset,  // only bumps when a changeset names it
    Auto,       // infers from conventional commits if no changeset present
}
```

This is a **per-package (or per-package-set) config field**, not a workspace-wide switch. §7.1 gives the precedence rule: *"`ReleaseTrigger::Auto` packages with no changeset get inferred severity from Conventional Commits since last tag... A changeset always wins over inference."*

That last clause is the actual answer to "can both apply at once": an `Auto`-trigger package defaults to release-please-style semantic-commit inference, but if you *do* drop a changeset on it, your explicit intent overrides the inference for that release. So the two models aren't mutually exclusive per package — `Auto` is really "infer by default, but purposeful override always wins."

§14's example config already demonstrates mixing both **across ecosystems in the same workspace**, which is exactly the case you'd actually want:

```toml
[[package-set]]
match = "crates/*"
release-trigger = "auto"        # release-please-style: infer from commits
publish-to = ["cratesIo"]

[[package-set]]
match = "packages/*"
release-trigger = "changeset"   # changesets-style: explicit intent only
publish-to = ["npm"]
```

And because severity aggregation (§7.1-§7.4) is unified regardless of where the severity came from, cross-ecosystem cascade works the same whether a dependency's bump was inferred or explicit — the graph doesn't care about provenance, only the resulting severity.

**One real gap this surfaces, worth flagging:** P1's byte-compat/rollback guarantee is scoped to `Changeset`-trigger packages only — the decision doc already noted "rollback is only lossless for `Changeset`-trigger packages" when discussing the 0.x-remap question. `Auto`-trigger packages never had a changesets-native form to roll back to, so that's an honest, not a hidden, limitation — but it should probably be one line in §4's principles rather than something only discoverable by cross-referencing two docs.

**The other gap:** the milestone list (§17) never actually schedules `callisto-conventional` — v0.1 ships `callisto-model` (where the `ReleaseTrigger::Auto` variant lives) but not the crate that parses conventional commits and makes `Auto` functional. So `Auto`/hybrid mode is designed for day one but isn't scheduled to actually work until whichever milestone picks up `callisto-conventional` — currently undefined. Want me to fold both of these (a principle-level note in §4, and slotting `callisto-conventional` into a milestone — v0.2 pairs naturally, since §6.3's empty-changeset validation already needs "commits/changes since last tag" plumbing) into `00-design.md` directly?

content.text:
The GH Actions research just landed — quick summary before the napi question: **release-please's PR-body pattern is better prior art than changesets' for callisto** (collapsible `<details>` per package instead of always-expanded sections, label-based idempotent PR lookup instead of branch-name-only, file-on-branch overflow instead of silently dropping changelog content when the body exceeds GitHub's 65536-char limit, and richer per-package job `outputs:` instead of just a package-name array). Confirms/refines callisto's existing `managedLabels` design rather than changing it. Nx Release has no PR-gated release concept at all, so it's not useful prior art here. I can fold this into `00-design.md` §12.2/§12.5 if you want.

Now, on napi/Rust+npm — honest assessment: **structurally solid, but not fully verified**, and there's a real gap in the milestone plan.

**What's actually well-covered:**
- The manifest-role axis (Canonical/Platform/Lockfile, §5.2) cleanly models the crate→N-platform-packages→main-package shape — Platform manifests inherit the parent's version rather than being independently versioned.
- Fixed groups (§7.5) give hard pre-mutation alignment checks, which is exactly what prevents the failure mode release-please's own `#2207` documents (two years unfixed: a Node project wrapping a Rust workspace where "bump everything together" silently doesn't happen because linked-versions and tag/identity resolution are two independently-evolved code paths that disagree).
- The plan ordering (§9.2, invariant 8 in §13) — Rust crates → npm platform packages → npm main packages, non-negotiable via config — correctly encodes the real constraint (`optionalDependencies` at exact versions means platforms must exist on the registry before the main package install resolves, or it 404s).
- §5.3's napi auto-derivation from `napi.targets` is explicitly scoped as "best-effort suggestion, not authoritative," which is the right posture given it's inferring from `@napi-rs/cli` config we don't control.

**What we haven't actually done:** we cited napi-rs's own release docs in Appendix A but never sent an agent to read them or the actual ecosystem's real-world practice. Everything napi-specific in the design is derived from first principles plus the *absence* of prior art (§2.1's comparison table literally says "Nothing" handles this case) — we've never checked what real napi-rs monorepos (napi-rs's own repo, or big consumers of it) actually do today as a workaround, which might surface a failure mode we haven't thought of.

**Three concrete open gaps, not yet resolved anywhere in the docs:**
1. **Do Platform manifests get their own git tag?** §9.2's `releases[]` array isn't explicit about whether N platform-package variants each get a tag or only the main package does. Tagging every platform variant seems clearly wrong (tag spam) but nothing currently says so.
2. **Cargo `workspace.dependencies` inheritance × fixed groups** — this is §18's Q2, already flagged as unresolved, and it's sharper for napi specifically: the crate's version lives in a workspace-inherited field, the main npm package's version lives in `package.json`, and a fixed group needs to keep both in lockstep through that inheritance indirection.
3. **Platform target list changing between releases** (a target added/dropped from `napi.targets`) — fixed-group alignment checking assumes a stable member set; nothing addresses what happens when the set itself changes.

Want me to run a targeted research pass — check napi-rs's own repo and any real polyglot-monorepo case studies for how they actually handle this today, and get a second opinion on gaps 1–3 — before we call napi "well-understood" for v0.3?

I don't think platform manifests get their onw git tags. They'd be attached to the overall "tool" right so it makes sense to keep things together.

Correct that we need to keep things in lock-step.

How should we handle added/dropped items from a fixed group set?

Right — that resolves gap 1 cleanly and it's consistent with the model: only the main npm package (and the crate, if separately published) get real tags; platform packages are dependents-in-lockstep, not independently released artifacts. Worth a one-line addition to §9.2/§13 to make that explicit rather than implicit.

For added/dropped targets, I'd apply the same pattern we already landed on for moon's project graph: **config stays authoritative, the external signal (`napi.targets`) becomes a non-authoritative cross-check, not a driver of mutation.** That's deliberate — §5.3 already decided not to re-couple to `@napi-rs/cli` internals every run, so `napi.targets` shouldn't silently rewrite group membership. Concretely:

**1. Detection is a diff, not a re-derivation.** On every `callisto version` run touching a napi-linked fixed group, cheaply re-read `napi.targets` from the main package's `package.json` and diff it against the fixed-group's configured `members`. Three outcomes: match (proceed), `napi.targets` has an entry `members` doesn't (target added), `members` has an entry `napi.targets` doesn't (target dropped).

**2. Both mismatches are warn-by-default / `--strict`-hard-fail** — the same shape §6.3's empty-changeset validation and the moon `declared_edges` cross-check already use, so this isn't a new UX pattern, just the established one applied again. Never auto-mutate `callisto.toml` from the diff — config changes should be a reviewable diff in the PR, not a silent rewrite. Extend `callisto init`'s existing "offer to write the derived group" behavior (§5.3) into the acceptance path: surface the diff, let the user accept it explicitly.

**3. A newly-added member needs one real exemption in the mutation logic.** §7.6 step 2's alignment check ("hard error if already divergent") would wrongly fire on a brand-new platform package sitting at whatever placeholder version napi-rs scaffolding gave it (e.g. `0.0.0`) versus the group's actual current version. The fix: **a member with no prior release tag is exempt from the divergence check** — it's not diverged, it's joining. Step 4 ("write platform manifests, inherit parent version") already unconditionally overwrites platform versions, so once it's a recognized group member, it just gets force-set to the group's target version on that release with no special-case mutation logic needed. The only new rule is the exemption in the *check*, not in the *write*.

**4. A dropped member has two distinct cases, not one:**
- **Still in `members` config, but the manifest file is gone** → hard error (P5: a config-declared required member silently missing on disk is a real problem, fail loudly).
- **File still present, but `napi.targets` no longer lists it** → the cross-check warning from (2), prompting the human to either delete the leftover package or accept the config update.
- Once actually removed from config *and* the manifest/package deleted, there's nothing further to do — no tag cleanup, no version-history concern, precisely because (per your correction) platform manifests were never independently tagged in the first place.

This is a small, self-contained addition — one new cross-check rule, one exemption clause in the existing alignment check, no new commands beyond extending `init`'s existing accept-the-diff flow. Want me to write this into `00-design.md` §7.5/§7.6/§13 now, along with the platform-tagging clarification from your first point?
Yes, write it into 00-design.md

input.new_string:
**Fixed** — members always share the exact version; validated pre-mutation (hard error if
already divergent). Used for napi main+platform coordination.

**Linked** — members share a version only when jointly releasing; independent version
lines otherwise.

**Platform manifests are never independently tagged.** Only the napi main package (and the
crate, if it's separately published to crates.io) represent a real release point in
`plan-publish`'s `releases[]` (§9.2) and get a git tag; the N platform packages are
dependents-in-lockstep, not independently released artifacts, so there is nothing to tag
per-platform and no orphan-tag cleanup to worry about when a platform is later dropped.

**Handling `napi.targets` drift (added/dropped platform targets).** A fixed group's
`members` list is config, and config is authoritative for what a version bump actually
touches — `napi.targets` is read every run purely as a cross-check (§5.3), never as a
membership source:

- **Target added to `napi.targets` but not yet in `members`** — warn by default (`--strict`
  hard-fails), same shape as §6.3's empty-changeset validation. Never auto-added to
  `callisto.toml`; the user accepts the diff via `callisto init`'s existing "offer to write
  the derived group" flow, which then shows up as a normal, reviewable config change.
- **`members` lists a platform no longer in `napi.targets`, but its manifest file is still
  present on disk** — same warn/`--strict` cross-check, prompting the human to either delete
  the leftover package directory or accept the config update removing it.
- **`members` lists a platform whose manifest file is missing entirely** — this is not a
  drift diagnostic, it's a hard error unconditionally: a config-declared required member
  that doesn't exist on disk fails loudly (P5) rather than being silently skipped.
- **A member actually removed from both `members` and disk** — no special handling needed;
  it simply stops participating in future bumps. Nothing to clean up, per the no-independent-
  tagging point above.

**New members are exempt from the pre-mutation divergence check.** A member with no prior
release tag (i.e., genuinely joining the group — freshly scaffolded by `@napi-rs/cli` at
whatever placeholder version it was given, e.g. `0.0.0`) is not "divergent" in the sense
§7.6 step 2 checks for; divergence is only a meaningful concept between two versions with
release history. Such a member is exempted from that check and is unconditionally force-set
to the group's target version the first time §7.6 step 4 writes platform manifests — no
separate initialization logic is needed, since inherit-parent-version already overwrites
whatever placeholder was there. After that first inclusion, the member is subject to the
normal alignment check on every subsequent run like any other group member.

192	## 4. Design principles
193	
194	**P1 — Byte-compatibility with `@changesets/cli`'s file format is a hard requirement.**
195	Same `.changeset/*.md` shape, same `pre.json` shape, same `bump_version` semantics
196	(including the "no 0.x-to-0.(x+1) remap on explicit major" behavior). One-commit adoption,
197	one-commit rollback. This is the adoption gate; nothing overrides it.
198	
199	**P2 — Statelessness for correctness; state only as a hint.** "Does this need publishing?"
200	is answered by comparing on-disk state to git tags, never by trusting a file that might not
201	survive a branch merge or a tool-version upgrade. Any state file callisto writes is
202	`.gitignore`d and never load-bearing for a correctness decision.
203	
204	**P3 — Idempotence per phase.** Every operation callisto performs is safe to re-run. A
205	partial failure followed by a retry does not double-apply anything.
206	
207	**P4 — Polyglot uniformity, including grammar and workspace concept, not just manifest
208	format.** Cargo, npm, and (when demand-gated ecosystems are added) Python/Go/Maven are all
209	"an ecosystem" behind the same traits. Adding one is bounded: one grammar impl, one
210	manifest impl, one identity-resolution note. Anywhere the design assumes SemVer implicitly,
211	that's a trait boundary in disguise and should be named as one.
212	
213	**P5 — Structural fixes over discipline.** When a class of failure is identified, the fix
214	belongs in code (a check, an invariant, a refusal to proceed) — not in a README section
215	telling people to remember something. See §13 for the concrete invariants this principle
216	has produced.
217	
218	**P6 — Release semantics live in the coordination core; every wrapper is a thin
219	dispatcher.** (Revised from an earlier "zero logic in the wrapper" phrasing, which was too
220	strong — wrappers legitimately contain orchestration logic like binary installation,
221	platform detection, and JSON-to-GHA-output translation. What they must never contain is
222	*release semantics*: computing bumps, resolving cascade, deciding publish order, writing
223	changelogs. If a wrapper needs to compute any of those, that's a missing capability in the
224	core, not something to write in the wrapper.)
225	
226	**P7 — Every boundary is explicit and testable.** Between the core and any integration
227	(moon, the Action, a future Nx plugin): a versioned, fixtured JSON/API contract. Between
228	callisto and upstream tools it shells out to (`git`, and whichever ecosystem tools it
229	queries): a runtime capability check with a clear error on mismatch, not a silent
230	assumption. Between callisto's own artifacts (e.g., a `setup-moon-callisto` composite
231	delegating to `callisto-action`): exact-pin delegation with an automated bump path, never
232	floating-major delegation between things we both own.

The evidence from release-please, Nx Release, semantic-release, and knope does *not* support Option B's premise — that callisto has three equally-weighted consumers — because callisto's own design has already decided the GitHub Action is a bash-composite that shells out to the CLI binary (§12.1), not an independent API consumer. Both critiques converge hard on the same root cause, which is itself the most useful finding: **§0.1's resolution never propagated.** Opus found direct evidence — the decision doc's own line-number citations into the spec are stale everywhere except its citation of §0.1, meaning ~105 lines of edits landed in the spec after the decision doc was written, but nobody went back and updated the sections downstream of §0.1 itself. Six places in the spec still say "open question" / "provisional" / "undecided," and §15 still specs the exact `MoonProjectGraphResolver` the decision doc said to delete for correctness reasons.

**Agreed by both models independently (highest confidence — fix these first):**

| # | Finding | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | §0.1 still "open" in 6 places; §15 still specs `MoonProjectGraphResolver`, which the decision doc proved can't work | Correctness bug |
| 2 | `callisto snapshot` — has a `published`-field JSON contract and is called a "publish path," directly contradicting §9's "callisto never publishes" reframe. Also drifts between flag (§8) and subcommand (§12), in no milestone, in no §11 command table | Contradicts core reframe |
| 3 | Three incompatible stories on who creates/pushes git tags (§9.1 says callisto creates, §9.3's own worked example has the *workflow* create them, §11 says `callisto tag` pushes) | Fable adds: this isn't cosmetic — if callisto tags at `version`-time and publish later fails, P2's stateless detection would wrongly conclude the release happened |
| 4 | `callisto-changelog` crate ships nothing in any milestone despite v0.1's `version` command requiring it (§7.6 step 7) | Milestone gap |
| 5 | §4's P1 scope note cites "§7.1's pre-major-inference discussion" — §7.1 has no such content; it only exists in the decision doc | Dangling reference, half-landed edit |
| 6 | `Manifest` is both a struct (§5.2) and an unrelated trait (§15) with no `role()` accessor; `DepEdge`/`DependencyEntry`/`DepKind`/`Severity`/`WorkspaceKind` used in signatures but never declared in §5 | Type drift |
| 7 | §14's config vocabulary (`patch\|minor\|always\|none`) doesn't map to §7.4's actual cascade modes (`OutOfRange`\|`Always`) | Unconfigurable-as-specced |
| 8 | §18 Q3 (`validate`: subcommand or flag?) still listed open while §11/§12.2 already hardcode the subcommand answer; also §18 Q2 (workspace-deps inheritance) says "must work from v0.1" while sitting in the open-questions list and absent from the v0.1 bullet | Spec disagrees with itself |
| 9 | **Pre-release mode × fixed-groups/napi-drift interaction is completely unspecified** — both ship in v0.3, neither says what happens when a napi target joins mid-pre-cycle, or whether alignment checks compare on-disk vs. `initialVersions` | Real design gap, not just drift |
| 10 | §13 invariant 6 is a leftover from the deleted publish-orchestrator design (asserts idempotence of "plan-consuming operations," which callisto no longer executes); invariant 12's wording is temporally impossible as written (plan is written *after* mutation, per §7.6's own step ordering) | Stale invariants |
| 11 | Decision-doc's concrete outputs (`ProjectLocator`, `DeclaredEdge`, plan types moving to MIT-licensed `callisto-model`, the wasmtime-CI rule, the #2207 one-function tag-resolution rule, parse-time fixed∩linked validation) never actually landed anywhere in the spec | Systemic — same root cause as #1 |

**High-value catches unique to one model** (worth trusting despite single-source — both are technically sharp, not speculative):

- **Opus only — group-forcing vs. cascade fixpoint ordering is never specified.** Forcing a fixed-group member to the group version can push it out of range for *its own* dependents, requiring another cascade pass. Whether group-forcing happens inside the fixpoint loop, once after convergence, or before it starts gives three different final version sets, and nothing picks one.
- **Opus only — `tag_template` is unparseable in general.** `last_tag_for` and §6.3 both need to invert a tag string back to `(package, version)`, but arbitrary user `{version}`-interpolated templates aren't generally invertible. This is a harder problem than "one function should resolve tags," which is all the decision doc asked for.
- **Fable only — §5.4's asymmetric dual-publish example may be unimplementable.** §5.2 says Case D is one `Package` with two `Canonical` manifests sharing *one* version (aggregated by max per §7.1). §5.4 then shows a changeset targeting `cargo/foo: patch` and `npm/foo: minor` asymmetrically — but there's no model slot for two sides of one package to actually diverge. Either Case D is secretly two `Package`s, or the §5.4 example doesn't mean what it appears to mean.
- **Fable only — pre-release mode × `Auto`-trigger is never specified**, and looks like a real functional bug: pre-mode idempotence works by tracking consumed changesets in `pre.json`'s `pre.changesets`, but `Auto`-trigger packages bump from conventional commits, which changesets-format `pre.json` has no field to record — so repeated `callisto version` runs in pre-mode would plausibly re-increment `Auto` packages on every run.
- **Fable only — §12.4 contradicts itself on `published-packages`' shape within 8 lines** (`[{name,version}]` vs. `{name,version,ecosystem,publishedTo}`) — the recommendation prose I added earlier was never reconciled with the line above it.

**The rest** (§17/§18 milestone timing gaps, misattributed principles on invariants 9/10, orphaned `PublishTarget::GitHubRelease`, `publishTo`/`publishedTo` naming drift, `--strict` flag reuse across unrelated checks, §2.2's stated scope discipline being contradicted by §5's fully-enumerated 13-variant `ManifestFormat` enum) are real but mechanical — worth fixing, lower stakes.

Some of these are pure editorial cleanup I can just do. But a few are genuine unresolved design decisions that need your call, not mine: **who creates tags and when** (I'd lean toward §9.3's version — tag after publish succeeds, since Fable's safety argument is right), **group-forcing vs. cascade ordering**, and **the Case D asymmetric-severity semantics**. Want me to fix the mechanical items now and then work through the open design decisions with you one at a time, or triage everything together first?
How do we address the issues the two models found?

I'll resolve the genuine design gaps myself (grounded in the existing principles, so each resolution traces to something already established) and fix the mechanical drift, then apply all of it to `00-design.md`. Let me work through this section by section.

27	
28	Callisto solves a problem every mature polyglot monorepo runs into eventually: you have
29	Rust crates, npm packages, and (increasingly) napi-bridged packages between them, and no
30	single existing tool understands version coordination across all three cleanly.
31	
32	- `@changesets/cli` is JS-only. Polyglot users work around this today by creating "proxy"
33	  `package.json` files for their Rust/Python packages so changesets treats them as
34	  versionable, then hand-writing a sync script that copies the bumped version out of
35	  `package.json` into `Cargo.toml`/`pyproject.toml` after the fact. This is a documented,

### 0.1 Resolved: Option C, narrowly defined

Everything in this document was, until this revision, designed with an implicit assumption:
callisto is a moon extension first, with a standalone CLI as a secondary surface. Research
into `release-please`'s actual architecture (see `docs/01-research-brief.md`) complicated
that assumption in a useful way: release-please ships as a **library** (the `release-please`
npm package exports a `Manifest` class and the releaser/plugin machinery directly) with
both its CLI and its GitHub Action built as thin consumers of that library. Neither the CLI
nor the Action contains coordination logic; both just call the library and wire up I/O.

That raised a real design fork for callisto — moon-first (Option A: core crates designed
around moon's project graph as a first-class input, standalone CLI a degraded fallback),
library-first (Option B: zero-moon-dependency core exposing a stable public Rust API / C
ABI, with moon, the Action, and the CLI as three symmetric consumers), or hybrid (Option C:
library-first internals, moon as the reference integration shipped and supported first).

**`docs/02-library-vs-moon-decision.md` resolved this**, against release-please, Nx
Release's v21 versioning rewrite, semantic-release, and knope as prior art, all independently
fact-checked and adversarially red-teamed before landing here. The verdict is **Option C**,
but narrower than "moon, the Action, and the CLI are three symmetric consumers" — that
premise is false in callisto's own design, since §12.1 already makes the Action a CLI
consumer (shells out to the `callisto` binary), not a library consumer. The real minimal
version of library-first is four CI-enforceable rules, not an API-design project:

1. **Zero moon in the dependency tree of the coordination core** (`callisto-format`,
   `callisto-model`, `callisto-graph`, `callisto-manifests`, `callisto-conventional`,
   `callisto-changelog`) — enforced in CI, not by convention.
2. **The core builds for `wasm32-wasip1` *and* passes its fixture suite under `wasmtime`
   with only the workspace root preopened** — a CI job from v0.1, before `callisto-moon`
   exists, because build-only conformance misses the runtime-only failures WASI's real
   filesystem API otherwise hides (compilation succeeding is not the same as working under
   moon's preopened-directory sandbox).
3. **Compute/apply split**, borrowed from release-please's `Manifest.buildPullRequests()`/
   `createPullRequests()`: every command is a pure function returning a plan value, plus a
   separate step that touches disk.
4. **The stable public contract is `--format json` on stdout** (§12.5), not a semver-stable

### 7.1 Aggregation

Load pending changesets → validate named packages exist → aggregate per-package severity
by max. `ReleaseTrigger::Auto` packages with no changeset get inferred severity from
Conventional Commits since last tag (`<type>!:`/`BREAKING CHANGE:` uppercase-only → major,
`feat` → minor, `fix`/`perf` → patch). A changeset always wins over inference.

**Pre-major inference (`callisto-conventional`, v0.2, referenced by P1's scope note in
§4).** `bump_version` (§6.2) stays rigid — no 0.x remap, no flag, no config path reaches it,
ever. That rigidity only has teeth for `Changeset`-trigger packages, because that's the only
trigger with a real `@changesets/cli` file to be byte-compatible *with*; `Auto`-trigger
inference has no changesets-native equivalent to diverge from. So the opt-in remap this
principle would otherwise forbid lives one layer up, entirely inside inference: an opt-in
per-package/per-group `pre-major-inference = "conservative"` setting that maps `breaking →
Severity::Minor` and (separately gated) `feat → Severity::Patch`, applied only when
producing a severity for an `Auto`-trigger package whose current on-disk version is `0.y.z`
with `y > 0`. Default off. Inert (no remap, tool says so explicitly) when the current
version is `0.0.z` or there is no prior tag — that exact boundary is where release-please's
own `bumpMinorPreMajor` has leaked bugs for years (its issues #2087/#2635), so it's a tested
case from day one, not an emergent one. The existing "a changeset always wins over
inference" rule composes for free: an explicit `major` in a changeset still produces the
real major bump regardless of this setting, since the setting only ever touches inferred
severities. Document the divergence from `@changesets/cli` loudly in the v0.4 migration
guide, in the same breath as the one-commit-rollback promise.

**Fixed-group severity union — resolves the group-forcing-vs-cascade-fixpoint ordering
question.** Before §7.4's cascade runs to fixpoint, any severity assigned (by changeset or
inference) to *any* member of a fixed group (§7.5) is unioned by max across every member of
that group. This is a single pre-step, not something interleaved with or run after the
fixpoint: by the time §7.4 starts, fixed-group members already carry identical target
severities, so the fixpoint treats them uniformly and correctly cascades their dependents in
one pass — no second pass is needed to "catch up" a group member the fixpoint moved. Given
identical starting severities and (per §7.5) identical aligned base versions, the members
necessarily converge on the same resulting version without any separate version-forcing
step at write time; §7.6 step 2's "alignment re-check" is therefore a verification that this
held, not a corrective write (the one exception remains the new-member exemption in §7.5,
which is a write, not a check).

last *stable* tag — so already-counted commits are naturally excluded without any new

for `Auto`-trigger packages, the same way they already are for `Changeset`-trigger ones.

840	
841	```bash
842	callisto version
843	git commit -am "chore: version packages"
844	
845	callisto plan-publish --format json > plan.json
846	
847	# Rust: topo-sorted from the plan
848	jq -r '.rustCrates[].name' plan.json | while read c; do cargo publish -p "$c"; done
849	
850	# npm: platforms first, mains second — the plan's structure already encodes this order
851	pnpm -r publish --filter "$(jq -r '.npmPlatformPackages[].name' plan.json | paste -sd, -)"
852	pnpm -r publish --filter "$(jq -r '.npmMainPackages[].name' plan.json | paste -sd, -)"
853	
854	# Tag on success — this is what closes the stateless-detection loop for next time
855	jq -r '.releases[] | "\(.tagName) \(.sha)"' plan.json | while read tag sha; do
856	  git tag "$tag" "$sha"
857	done
858	git push --tags
859	```
860	
861	The tag creation on success is the signal that makes next run's stateless detection work —
862	no callisto command "reads back" what got published; the tag existing (or not) at the
863	expected version is the only source of truth.

870	registry, the ecosystem tool's own refusal is the safety net — cheap, correct, and not
871	callisto's problem to duplicate.

result.output:
140	### 2.2 Ecosystem priority — committed vs demand-gated
141	
142	An earlier draft of this design treated "support every language" as an implicit goal and
143	grew scope accordingly (Python, Go, Java, Scala, C#, Ruby, Deno all got design attention).
144	An adversarial review of that draft concluded the scope had outrun the addressable market:
145	callisto's actual niche is narrow (moon workspaces, changesets-format preference, napi
146	coordination), and building for languages nobody in that niche has asked for is waste.
147	
148	Revised posture:
149	
150	| Ecosystem | Status |
151	|---|---|
152	| Rust / Cargo | **Committed, v0.1** |
153	| npm (npm/pnpm/yarn workspaces) | **Committed, v0.1** |
154	| napi platform packages | **Committed, v0.3** |
155	| Python (uv/hatch/poetry, PEP 440) | Real, tractable, **demand-gated** — not scheduled until a user asks. Design supports it (§7.7) but it is not release-blocking for any v0.1–v0.4 milestone. |
156	| Go modules | Real, tractable (git-tag-only publish, no registry backend needed), **demand-gated**. |
157	| Maven / Gradle-catalog / sbt-version-file | Tractable under the versioning-coordinator posture (§9) because callisto never touches Maven Central/Sonatype's publish machinery — only version bumps and dependency-graph coordination. **Demand-gated.** |
158	| NuGet, Deno/JSR, Ruby | Tractable, **demand-gated**. |
159	| Gradle/sbt imperative DSL write-back (`build.gradle`, `build.sbt`) | Read-only if ever built; write-back requires AST-aware editing of Turing-complete build scripts and is **not planned**. |
160	| Java/Scala versioning grammar in the abstract | Supported by the trait design (see §7.7) whenever an ecosystem needs it — Maven's version-comparison rules are well-specified and portable. |
161	| C / vcpkg / Conan | **Not building.** C libraries version through distro packaging, not per-package registry publishes. The polyglot-monorepo-with-coordinated-releases shape callisto addresses doesn't exist for C. |
162	
163	The trait boundaries in §7 and §15 are designed so that adding any demand-gated ecosystem
164	is bounded work (one grammar impl, one manifest impl, one identity-resolution note) — not
165	because we're building toward all of them, but because the abstraction should not make any
166	of them artificially hard if a real user shows up needing one.
167

input.new_string:
**Linked** — members share a version only when jointly releasing; independent version
lines otherwise. **"Jointly releasing" means jointly *named*, not jointly *cascaded to*** —
this is the deliberate difference from fixed groups' §7.1 severity-union pre-step, which
does apply to cascade-induced bumps. A changeset or inference assigning severity to ≥2
linked members in the same run counts as joint and unions their severity by max, exactly
like a fixed group would; a cascade-induced bump (§7.4) landing on only one linked member,
with the rest untouched, does **not** pull its linked siblings along — cascade is a
mechanical consequence of a dependency edge, not an expression of release intent, and
"jointly releasing" is about intent. A linked member that diverges via cascade this way
simply starts (or continues) an independent version line until a future changeset/inference
event touches ≥2 members again.

**Platform manifests are never independently tagged.**
